name: PPT: Communication With Elderly And Patient With Special Needs
text: Communication with Elderly Patients By Somaya Madkour 1 What are the factors that can affect the ability of elderly to communicate effectively? The aging process can cause changes in physical, cognitive, and social aspects. Physical challenges: memory problems, speech difficulties, or hearing difficulties. Social challenges: feelings of loneliness, social isolation, or feelings of being unappreciated So A communication approach that acknowledges and respects their feelings is very important to help the elderly feel heard and cared for. Avoid paternalistic attitudes that might limit their participation in making decisions about their own health. Be a good listener, respect older people's perspectives, and seek a deeper understanding of their needs and preferences. Empathy and Patience listening Active Listening The elderly often experience hearing loss or certain cognitive problems so Be attentive and give the elderly patient time to express themselves fully without interruption. Reflection Repeat or conclude what the elderly have said to show you understand and validate their experiences. Establish Trust A trusting relationship is essential for effective collaboration in treatment and care. 4 A physician recently saw an elderly patient with parkinsonism and depression. The patient began by noting that he had numerous bad experiences with physician and health care system. The physician listened attentively and used rapport building skills in the initial 5 minutes. Although the patient had numerous criticism of other physicians, the interviewer did not have to join in this criticism to build rapport. Empathetic communication is sufficient It seems like you have had some troubling experiences with the medical system ( reflection) I can understand how you felt insignificant and unimportant ( legitimation) I want you to know that I care about your difficulties and I will do my best to work with you to develop a plan to bring you some relief ( support and partnership) Adapting Language Simple, Clear Language Avoid complex medical terminology and speak in a way that is easy for the elderly to understand. By using simple language, ----older people are more likely to understand messages better and feel more confident in dealing with care and treatment. --understand the treatment options available, the risks and benefits and allows them to participate actively in making decisions about their own health. Multiple Learning Styles Use visual aids including diagrams, pictures and computers programmers with written and verbal instructions to enhance understanding Shared Decision-Making Ensure the patient can actively participate in decisions about their own health care. 6 Create Comfortable Environment 1-Reduce Distractions Minimize noise, as they distract the elderly and make it difficult for them to concentrate or listen properly ---- provide good lighting, as it help them see your facial expressions and body language, which are important in communication. ----ensure the physical space is accommodating. 2-Friendly Attitude Greet them with a smile and speak in a gentle tone of voice to let them feel more relaxed and open to talking 3-Avoid Pressure It is important to respect the privacy of the elderly and provide opportunities for them to speak without pressure. Speak attentively and don’t ask personal questions if the elderly don't want to talk about it. 7 Engaging the Elderly Open-Ended Questions Open questions to provide more detailed and in-depth answers than just "yes" or "no". You can better understand what is most important to them in care and how you can help meet those needs. --Encourage the patient to express their needs, concerns, and emotions freely. Reflective Listening Demonstrate understanding by summarizing because of hearing, vision, cognitive and communication difficulties, elderly patient may not succeed in transmitting information accurately to the physician the first time. Empathetic Support Validate the patient's experiences and work together to address their challenges. Collaborative Approach Involve the patient as an equal partner in their own health care decisions. 8 Physician: With so much going on your life, let me repeat back what I have just heard to make sure I have understood your problem correctly if a family member or caregiver is present Physician: I have spent some time with your ( spouse, father…) please let me know how you think he or she has been doing Respect for Autonomy and Participation Empower Patients Involve elderly patients in decision-making about their care to foster confidence and an active role in their health. Encourage Participation Patients who participate in decisions tend to better understand their conditions and treatment options. Build Trust They will ask more questions, seek information, and consider all options better, which can ultimately lead to more informed treatment decisions that match their preferences. 10 Convey realistic expectations Honesty is Key Provide clear, honest information about health conditions and prognosis to build trust. Hiding or withholding important information does not respect their rights to get a clear and complete explanation about their health. Manage Expectations By conveying clear and realistic information about health conditions, the elderly and their families can make appropriate preparations and plan treatment better. Avoid false hope, which can lead to disappointment if expectations are not met. Empower Decisions Transparent communication allows elderly patients to make informed, preference-aligned treatment decisions. 11 Overcome feelings of loneliness and isolation Effective communication provides an opportunity for older people to talk and interact with others, especially if they are living in a care facility or facing social isolation. . Feeling Valued Elderly patients feel more meaningful when they are heard and involved. Remaining Engaged Meaningful interactions help the elderly stay connected to the world around them. Social Connection 12 Motivate and provide support Acknowledge Effort Praise and recognition for dealing with health challenges can boost the elderly's enthusiasm. Offer Encouragement Emotional support from medical personnel is just as valuable as medical care. Inspire Hope Motivating the elderly to keep fighting can significantly improve their quality of life. 13 Clear Instructions Tailored Guidance Provide simple, step-by-step instructions for treatments, medications, and lifestyle changes. Visual Aids Use diagrams, pictures, or demonstration videos to supplement verbal instructions. Patient Adherence Clear communication promotes better understanding and adherence to treatment plans. 14 Involving Caregivers Collaborative Care Engage family members and caregivers in discussions to promote understanding and support. Tailored Approach Caregiver input can help personalize treatment plans for improved effectiveness. Enhanced Adherence Caregiver involvement can ensure treatment plans are properly followed and monitored. 15 Communication with Patients with Special Needs 16 These populations have a wide range of cognitive, expressive , receptive and physical capacities. So, it is important for healthcare providers to be aware of these challenges and to adapt their communication style accordingly. Communication Challenges Faced by Patients with Special Needs Speech or language disorders: They may have difficulty articulating words or understanding spoken language. Hearing or vision impairments: Have difficulty communicating with others if they cannot see or hear what is being said. Cognitive disabilities: Have difficulty understanding complex medical information or making decisions about their care. Mental health conditions: Have difficulty communicating their thoughts and feelings. Cultural or linguistic barriers: People who speak a different language or come from a different culture may have difficulty communicating with their healthcare providers. These healthcare communication barriers can be due to language barriers, cultural differences in communication styles, or lack of familiarity with the healthcare system. In all of these conditions it difficult to communicate their needs and preferences to their healthcare providers. 17 Communication with those with Impaired Hearing 1 Get Attention Gain the patient's attention before speaking, such as through touch. Minimize background noise and distractions 2 Enhance Visibility Facing the patient directly in a well-lit environment to facilitate lip-reading. 3 Adjust Speech Speak clearly, at a moderate pace, and avoid shouting. 18 Communication with those with Impaired Hearing 4 Non Verbal Communication The use gestures, Facial expressions and body movements can provide additional information in communication, especially for the elderly, who rely on body language to understand the context of the conversation 5 Offer Choices Ask the patient to suggest strategies for improved communication (e.g., speaking toward better ear). 6 Simple Language Simplify language (i.e., do not use slang but do use short, simple sentences), as appropriate 19 Assist the patient in acquiring a hearing aid or assistive listening device If the person uses an assistive hearing device (hearing aid), ensure that it is readily available to the person and in working order and that he uses it. After delivering the message, Be sure to confirm whether the senior has understood what you said. Ask the person for feedback or to repeat what you have said to assess understanding. If you do not understand something that is said, ask the person to repeat it or to write it down. Do not pretend to understand if you do not 20 Hearing Evaluation & Rehabilitation Hearing Assessment Refer patients for evaluation and treatment of hearing loss by an audiologist or specialist. If you are speaking through a sign language interpreter, pause occasionally to allow the interpreter time to translate completely and accurately. Talk directly to the person who is assisted by a sign interpreter, not to the interpreter, even if the person is looking at the interpreter and does not make eye contact with you. 21 Communication with those with Impaired vision 1 Get Attention Identify yourself when entering the patient’s space 2 Provide adequate room lighting and Provide magnifying devices 3 Patient comfort Ensure the patient’s eyeglasses or contact lenses have current prescription, are cleaned, and stored properly when not in use 22 Communication with those with Impaired vision 3 Non verbal communication Touch the person’s arm lightly when you speak so that he or she knows to whom you are speaking before you begin. Face the person and speak directly to him. 4 Suitable environment Minimize glare (i.e., offer sunglasses or draw window covering) Provide educational materials in large print 5 Tone of voice Use a normal tone of voice (avoid shouting). 23 Communication with those with Impaired Speech Step 1 Eliminate background noise and distractions to minimize excess noise and decrease emotional distress and Instruct the patient to speak slowly Step 2 Phrase questions so the patient can answer using a simple “Yes” or “No,” being aware that patients with aphasia may provide automatic responses that are incorrect Step 3 Be patient because it may take the person extra time to communicate Monitor the patient for frustration, anger, depression, or other responses to impaired speech capabilities and Repeat what the patient said to ensure accuracy 24 Step 4 Provide alternative methods of speech communication (e.g., writing tablet, flash cards, eye blinking, communication board with pictures and letters, hand signals or gestures, and computer) Step 5 Nod of the head or blink to indicate agreement or disagreement with what you have asked or said. • To obtain information quickly, ask short questions that require brief answers or a head nod Step 6 stand in front of the patient while speaking, listen attentively, present one idea or thought at a time, speak slowly but avoid shouting, use written communication, or ask family’s assistance in understanding the patient’s speech) Communication with those with Impaired Speech 25 Recommendations for Communicating with Patients with Intellectual, Cognitive or Developmental Disabilities Be prepared to repeat the same information more than once in different ways. When asking questions, phrase them without suggesting desired or preferred responses as some people with intellectual, cognitive or developmental disabilities may tell you what they think you want to hear. Give exact instructions. For example, “You will see the nurse at 10:30,” rather than “Come back to see the nurse in 15 minutes.” Treat adults with intellectual, cognitive or developmental disabilities as adults. Adjust your method of communication as necessary depending on the individual's responses to you. Use simple, direct sentences or supplementary visual forms of communication, such as gestures, diagrams, or demonstrations, if indicated. Use concrete, specific language. When possible, use words that relate to things you both can see. Avoid using directional terms such as right, left, east, or west. Do not pretend to understand if you do not. Ask the person to repeat what was said. Be patient, flexible, and supportive. Do not assume that the person will be able to read well; some may not read at all. Be respectful, kind, and don’t talk down to them or their loved ones. Maintain eye contact and a welcoming demeanor that invites communication. Understand there may be a healthy fear of healthcare personnel. We must maintain an open dialogue and convey that the patient’s thoughts, ideas, and concerns are important and welcome. Avoid giving too many directions at one time, which may be confusing. Eliminate distractions and minimize background noise if possible. Avoid sensory overload by providing information gradually and clearly. Provide information in written or verbal form if that is the person’s preference. Recognize that the person may need to have directions repeated and may take notes to help remember directions or the sequence of tasks. He or she may also benefit from watching a task demonstrated. Recommendations for Communicating with Patients with Intellectual, Cognitive or Developmental Disabilities Down Syndrome A 30-year-old male patient with Down syndrome is admitted to your unit. He’s articulate and appears to be very high functioning. His caregiver is at the business office addressing his insurance information while you begin your assessment. As you’re asking the patient questions, you realize that he has some learning deficits that are impeding the interview. You wait for the caregiver to return so you can collaborate on the admission forms and health history. You involve the patient in every step and formulate questions to his cognitive needs as possible Down syndrome can result in in a broad range of mild, moderate, or severe cognitive and physical delays Each patient is unique in his abilities and limitations, and care should be tailored to individual needs. When providing care for a patient with Down syndrome, tailor care to the patient’s developmental age rather than his or her actual age. Talk to the patient’s caregivers and ask questions so you can understand where your patient is developmentally. 28 Autism Spectrum Disorder Common nonpharmacologic interventions, such as decreasing environmental stimuli by reducing noise and distractions (such as the TV), can often greatly reduce the patient’s anxiety. Having the family provide familiar items may also reduce anxiety. It’s best to have the same healthcare provider care for the patient during each visit because patients with autism spectrum disorders do better with comfortable routines, and familiar faces and places. Patients with an autism spectrum disorder can present a challenge. Many children and adults with autism spectrum disorders have difficulty communicating with words that they’re becoming frustrated, anxious, or uncomfortable. They may begin humming, pacing, or yelling. Ask the patient and his or her caregiver about activities of daily living routines to minimize anxiety and frustration. You’re working in the ED of a busy Level-1 trauma facility when a 17-year-old patient with an autism spectrum disorder arrives. He presents with tachycardia and is growing increasingly anxious. His parents state that the patient doesn’t like the hemodynamic alarms that are audible in the distance. He’s having great difficulty communicating his abdominal pain symptoms and begins rapidly rocking back and forth in his chair. You consider that the patient is experiencing too much environmental stimuli, contributing to his anxiety. You move the patient to an area that has decreased environmental stimuli to help calm him so you can proceed with your physical assessment. Many patients experience mental disorders, such as paranoid schizophrenia, clinical depression, and bipolar disorder. These disorders can impact the patient’s quality of life, causing unusual shifts in mood, energy, and activity levels, and affecting the ability to carry out daily tasks and engage in social or occupational activities that he once enjoyed. There are what is called “ Negative symptoms” of reduced motivation, social withdrawal, and blunted effects that may have a major impact on the quality of life Communicating with Patients with Psychiatric/Mental Health Disabilities Recommendations for Communicating with Patients with Psychiatric/Mental Health Disabilities Approach the person as you would anyone else; speak directly to the person, using clear, simple communication. & Offer to shake hands when introduced. Treat persons who are adults as adults. Use the same good manners in interacting with a person who has a psychiatric/mental health disability that you would with anyone else. Do not make decisions for the person or assume that you know the person’s preferences. Several short interviews may be preferred than one long interview Make eye contact, and be aware of your own body language. Like others, people with psychiatric health disabilities will sense your discomfort. & Listen attentively, and wait for the person to finish speaking. If needed, clarify what the person has said. Recommendations for Communicating with Patients with Psychiatric/Mental Health Disabilities Although there are similar signs and symptoms with some mental disorders, remember that no two patients are alike. Be respectful of this and ask questions, investigate, and show sincere interest and a desire to help the patient address his or her individual needs. Do not pretend to understand if you do not. Ask the person to repeat what was said. Be patient, flexible, and supportive. Be calm, respectful, non judgmental and empathic Recognize that a person with psychiatric/mental health disabilities often has the same needs, dreams, and desires as anyone else. Recognize that interpersonal detachment of the patient may be a coping mechanism and the medical interview can be very stressful Step 1 Keep in mind that the personal space of a person with a disability includes the person’s wheelchair, scooter, crutches, walker, or other mobility aid. Step 2 Do not push or move a person’s wheelchair or grab a person’s arm to provide assistance without asking first. Step 3 When speaking to a person seated in a wheelchair or scooter, sit so that you and the person are at the same eye level. Communication with those with Mobility Limitations 34 Step 4 When giving directions to people with mobility limitations, consider distance, weather conditions, and physical obstacles such as stairs. Step 5 Shake hands when introduced to a person with a disability. People who have limited hand use or who wear an artificial limb do shake hands Communication with those with Mobility Limitations 35 Finally respect the patient's autonomy and dignity when communicating with them. This means acknowledging and honoring their rights, choices, and preferences. You can also use person-first or identity- People first language puts the person before the disability. For example: • Say “people with disabilities” instead of “disabled or handicapped.” • Say “s/he has autism” instead of “s/he is autistic.” • Say “s/he has an intellectual disability or cognitive disability” instead of “s/he is mentally retarded.” • Say “a person who uses a wheelchair” instead of “confined to a wheelchair.” Respect the Patient’s Autonomy and Dignity Collaborate with other professionals and resources when communicating with patients with disabilities. This means working with interpreters, translators, specialists, or advocates who can assist you and the patient. You can also refer the patient to relevant organizations, programs, or services that can support their communication needs. Collaborating with other professionals and resources can improve the quality, efficiency, and effectiveness of communication. Collaborate with Other Professionals and Resources THANK YOU 38

Be Prepared • Expect emotions. • Stay calm. • Plan for how you will deal. • Monitor what you think and feel • Practice self-regulation. • Turn the confrontation to conversation. • Know when NOT to have conversation (when emotions are too intense). 2. Maintain eye contact. Listen without interrupting, use clarifying statements or paraphrasing. Avoid trying to make a situation better when it is grave as saying, “I’m sure things will not be as bad as you think.” 3. Six Second Rule: Avoid escalation of conversation Well, it didn’t work because you waited too long to get help When your own emotions start to boil in response to anger, wait at least 6 seconds or more to calm down. • Avoid being defensive/blaming e.g. “.” • Gather your thoughts and use skills such as “tell me more” or empathic/validating responses. 22 4. Tell me more Tell me more about your husband. What happened after that? 23 5. Empathizing and validating to: I can see you weren’t expecting this It’s very stressful, isn’t it? It must be hard to come here every week I can see how difficult it is for you 24 AVOID I know how you feel. I feel your pain. It’s going to be alright. When your own emotions start to boil in response to anger, wait at least 6 seconds or more to calm down. • Avoid being defensive/blaming e.g. “.” • Gather your thoughts and use skills such as “tell me more” or empathic/validating responses. 25 6. Angry patient 1. Remain calm 2. Verbally comment on what you have observed I see you're angry; can we talk about it? I would be upset in your situation, but let's focus on how I can help you You entered the room, and the patient appears impatient Apologize for the delay while introducing yourself Sit or stand level with the patient, Make eye contact often, and try not to appear rushed If tests are required, give realistic estimates of how long they will take You feel yourself becoming angry or frustrated Do not deny your feelings, Honesty and sincerity will usually be rewarded. Find an excuse to leave the bedside for a few minutes before saying something you may regret later. I'm doing my best, but nothing seems to satisfy you try to identify what caused your reaction and formulate a strategy. 30 You feel yourself threatened/unsafe End the interaction This conversation is making me feel uncomfortable right now. I don’t feel safe right now and can’t continue this conversation.” 31 Switch strategies Sometimes you need to take command, other times, to compromise. She raises her voice and demands immediate attention, making the waiting room tense. The main issue: Angry Patient What should the healthcare provider's initial response be to Ms. Lee's anger? A) Respond with equal frustration and explain the busy schedule. B) Apologize for the wait and acknowledge her frustration. C) Ignore her complaints and proceed with the medical consultation. D) Ask her to leave if she cannot calm down. B The main issue: Angry Patient How can the healthcare provider effectively de-escalate the situation with Ms. Lee? A) Remain silent and let her vent without interruption. B) Tell her to calm down and wait her turn. C) Listen actively, validate her feelings, and provide a solution. D) Suggest she finds another clinic if she is dissatisfied. C Case Scenario Mr. Brown demands an unnecessary MRI scan. He read about its diagnostic value on the internet. Now, he is believing that it is the only way to diagnose his minor back pain despite the physician's recommendation for a more conservative approach. Expert patient through the Internet How should the physician address Mr. Brown's demand for an unnecessary MRI? A) Order the MRI to avoid conflict. B) Dismiss his concerns and refuse to discuss it further. C) Explain the rationale for the recommended approach and the risks of unnecessary tests. D) Refer him to another physician who might comply with his request. C Expert patient through the Internet What is an appropriate way to ensure Mr. Brown feels heard while maintaining professional integrity? A) Agree with everything Mr. Brown says to keep him satisfied. B) Provide detailed explanations and engage him in shared decision-making. C) Avoid discussing his concerns and focus on other health issues. D) Give in to his demands to avoid potential complaints. B 2. Motivational interview (MI) Definition: MI is a collaborative patient-centered directive method for enhancing intrinsic motivation to change by exploring and resolving ambivalence. Ambivalence • A state of mind in which a person has coexisting conflicting feelings, thoughts, and actions about a particular behavior. • Ambivalence maintains the gap between what people know and what they do. I should ---- BUT It is often marked by language such as a “but” in the middle as “I should change, but --- 42 Ambivalence • Interpreting ambivalence as denial, carelessness or resistance increases friction between you and your patient. • Ambivalence is normal and does not mean that a person is unmotivated. • It is important to understand and accept your patient's ambivalence because ambivalence is often the central problem. I should ---- BUT Ambivalence maintains the gap between what people know and what they do. It is often marked by language such as a “but” in the middle as “I should change, but --- 43 Goal of MI: The goal of MI is to help people see discrepancies between their present behaviors and broader goals through the identification, examination, and resolution of ambivalence about changing behavior. Thus, it is of value with difficult patient who resist to change and non-compliant with therapy. Spirit of MI is based on Collaboration Autonomy Evocation Spirit of MI is based on: Collaboration – MI rests on a collaborative partnership. Instead of directing the passive patient in what to do, there is an active collaborative conversation and joint decision-making process. This is particularly vital in health behavior change, because ultimately only the patient can make the change. Spirit of MI is based on: b. Evocation – listening and eliciting MI evoke from patients what they already have and activate their own motivations for change through connecting health behavior change with what patients care about, with their own values and concerns. 1) Where are you right now in …… ? 2)Where would you like to be? 3)What is currently preventing this happening? Spirit of MI is based on: c. Autonomy – Decision making is left to the patient Practitioners may inform, advise, even warn, but ultimately it is the patient who decides what to do. Autonomy is key in facilitating lasting change. There is something inherent in human nature that resists being coerced and told what to do. So, it is the professional’s responsibility to respect the patient’s ability to choose and accept that people make choices for themselves. 48 Principles of MI: 1. Resisting the righting reflex – • A patient’s response to the righting reflex is feeling not heard, not-understood, helpless, trapped and oppositional. • So instead, allow patients to explore both sides of their ambivalence to able to give reasons for change. Principles of MI: 2. Understand and explore the patient’s motivation- What is it that they want?/ Exploring DARN: Desire – Determine the patients desire to change (when desire is low, this is a signal to move back to following – reflect the resistance) Ability – How does the patient see her ability to change? (Ruler – From 1-10 with one being completely unable and ten being completely able, where do you see your ability?) Reasons –why they should change? (Pros vs. Cons) Need – why they need to change? 50 Principles of MI: 3. Listen with empathy Acceptance facilitates change. Skillful reflective listening is fundamental. Remember ambivalence is expected and normal Desire – Determine the patients desire to change (when desire is low, this is a signal to move back to following – reflect the resistance) Ability – How does the patient see her ability to change? (Ruler – From 1-10 with one being completely unable and ten being completely able, where do you see your ability?) Reasons –why they should change? (Pros vs. Cons) Need – why they need to change? 51 Principles of MI: 4. Empower – support self-efficacy- encouraging hope and optimism Once the patient has expressed his own desire to change, told you their confidence in being able to make the change, and told you reasons - then it is time to start taking steps to change. An example of a good directing style is using an Elicit-Provide-Elicit  Elicit - Can I tell you more about how to ..-Would you like me to tell you more about….  Provide – Give information  Elicit – Is there anything else on …. 52 Motivational good directive style MI Communication Styles: MI starts with a 1) listening 2) guiding (exploring options). 3) directive (giving advice). If you move into directing too soon, the chances for behavior change go down considerably. OARS is a brief way to remember the basic approach used in Motivational Interviewing Open Ended Questions: we ask questions the answer to which is change talk, we want the person talk about change. Affirmations: emphasizing patient’s past experiences that demonstrate strength, success, or power can prevent discouragement. Reflections: Helping people to say their arguments and then hearing them back makes them more familiar with what they believe. Summaries: Summaries reinforce what has been said, show that you have been listening carefully, and prepare to move on. 55 Case Scenario Dr. Smith is treating Mr. Johnson, a patient with diabetes. Despite repeated advice, Mr. Johnson continues to neglect his medication and dietary restrictions, leading to uncontrolled blood sugar levels. Dr. Smith is frustrated but needs to find an effective way to communicate the importance of adherence to the treatment plan. The main issue: Non-compliant patient What is the most ethical approach for Dr. Smith to take in discussing Mr. Johnson's non-compliance? A) Scold Mr. Johnson for not following the treatment plan. B) Express understanding of the challenges and explore the reasons for non-compliance. C) Threaten to discontinue care if Mr. Johnson does not adhere to the treatment plan. D) Ignore the issue and continue prescribing medication as usual. B Case Scenario Mr. Brown demands an unnecessary MRI scan. He read about its diagnostic value on the internet. Now, he is believing that it is the only way to diagnose his minor back pain despite the physician's recommendation for a more conservative approach. Expert patient through the Internet How should the physician address Mr. Brown's demand for an unnecessary MRI? A) Order the MRI to avoid conflict. B) Dismiss his concerns and refuse to discuss it further. C) Explain the rationale for the recommended approach and the risks of unnecessary tests. D) Refer him to another physician who might comply with his request. C Expert patient through the Internet What is an appropriate way to ensure Mr. Brown feels heard while maintaining professional integrity? A) Agree with everything Mr. Brown says to keep him satisfied. B) Provide detailed explanations and engage him in shared decision-making. C) Avoid discussing his concerns and focus on other health issues. D) Give in to his demands to avoid potential complaints. B Case Scenario Ms. Patel has a history of medical anxiety and expresses distrust in the proposed treatment plan, fearing potential side effects and questioning the necessity of the intervention. The Distrustful Patient How can the healthcare provider address Ms. Patel's medical anxiety effectively? A) Ignore her anxiety and focus solely on the medical facts. B) Suggest she seek psychiatric help and avoid discussing her fears. C) Incorporate strategies like motivational interviewing to explore her concerns and support her. D) Reassure her without providing detailed explanations to save time. C
